description:
We are HDMK team, in which members with huge ambition in Space and Computer Science engage in the path of exploration.

Our team is composed of four members: Ha Duyen Minh Khoi from Kim Lien High School, Ha Hoang Thu from Dinh Cong Secondary School, Ha Duyen Hung from Hanoi University of Science and Technology, and Ha Duyen Manh from Le Loi High School. Our guiding principles are Horizons, Deep Mission, and Kinetic
summary:
Annually, there are dozens of storms approaching northern and central Vietnam, causing severe damage. In emergency cases, victims cannot communicate with rescue teams.
At school, students learn a lot about orbit, energy, radio waves without any practical experiments. They often do not really know the applications.
ORBIT 72 is a browser-based game in which players design, launch, and operate a constellation of small satellites (CubeSats) to maintain emergency communication for 72 hours following a superstorm that has struck the damaged region. It is easily understood through the model "Build a satellite. Beat the storm. Keep everyone connected"
In this game, players experience six stages of mission. We have developed the program so that every decision has a visible consequence: players accept a contract, build a CubeSat, choose its orbit and rocket, hold a Go/No-Go poll, run 72 hours of mission control and receive a five-star debrief. Up to four players can work together in distinct roles. Mass, power, budget, data, communications and orbital lifetime must all be balanced, and NASA GPM IMERG rainfall data from Typhoon Yagi (2024) shapes the score. ORBIT 72 helps students see why a real space mission is a chain of trade-offs. It helps address the challenges above due to its high practical applicability, helping players learn how to use their knowledge of mathematics and physics to solve problems in their own local area and can be a solutions for confronting climate change.
details:
ORBIT 72 — Keep Them Connected is an interactive, browser-based space mission design simulation created by Team HDMK for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Grounded in a real-world emergency event—Typhoon Yagi in September 2024, which knocked out power and disconnected 6,285 mobile base stations across 15 provinces in Northern Vietnam—the game challenges players to design, launch, and operate an emergency CubeSat constellation to restore critical SOS communications during the vital first 72 hours after landfall.

What It Does & How It Works

The game places players in the shoes of aerospace engineers and mission controllers, guiding them through the end-to-end lifecycle of a real space mission:

  1. System Design & Trade-Off Analysis: Players configure their CubeSats by balancing strict engineering constraints—mass, power generation, battery capacity, and radio frequency payloads—referencing real-world specifications from NASA’s Small Spacecraft State-of-the-Art (SOA) report.
  2. Orbit & Launch Selection: Players select launch vehicles and orbital parameters (such as altitude and inclination), confronting the real-world physics of coverage windows, revisit rates, and orbital plane mechanics.
  3. Mission Control & Go/No-Go Review: In a 4-role multiplayer mode modeled after a real mission control room, team members evaluate telemetry and readiness before holding a collective Go/No-Go vote to authorize launch.
  4. 72-Hour Live Disaster Operations: Once in orbit, players actively manage their satellite constellation over a simulated 72-hour post-typhoon window—relaying emergency SOS messages from isolated communes in Northern Vietnam while reacting to dynamic environmental hazards, including real rainfall attenuation driven by NASA GPM IMERG precipitation data and space weather disruptions from NASA DONKI solar storm datasets.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Bridging Theory and Real-World Engineering: Students often learn orbital mechanics, power budgets, and radio wave propagation purely as abstract formulas. ORBIT 72 transforms those equations into tangible engineering trade-offs where every design choice directly determines whether an isolated community can reach rescue teams.
  • Accessible STEM Education: Built as a free, open-source, browser-based game with an offline-capable version, it removes hardware and internet barriers, allowing classrooms and students anywhere—even in areas with unstable connectivity—to experience authentic space mission design.
  • Raising Disaster Resilience Awareness: By anchoring the simulation in Vietnam’s actual telecommunications vulnerability during Typhoon Yagi, the project highlights how space technology directly supports terrestrial disaster response and public safety.

Creativity & Key Differentiators

  • Localized, Real-World Stakes: Rather than using generic sci-fi scenarios or universal ideas, the mission is rooted in a real national crisis in Vietnam, giving the engineering problem immediate human relevance.
  • The "Orbital Plane" Insight: The game intuitively teaches a common misconception in satellite design—that launching more satellites into the exact same orbital plane does not provide continuous regional coverage—requiring players to think spatially in three dimensions.
  • Collaborative Control-Room Dynamics: The 4-role multiplayer structure mirrors real aerospace teamwork, requiring communication, role specialization, and consensus under time pressure.

Key Factors Considered During Development

  • Scientific & Engineering Authenticity: Our technical mentor guided the team in translating actual NASA datasets and Small Spacecraft SOA hardware parameters into accurate yet playable physics models, ensuring educational credibility without overwhelming new players.
  • Reliability & Quality Assurance: To guarantee a smooth experience during live demonstrations and classroom use, the codebase was validated with over 300 automated tests covering orbital mechanics, power calculations, and mission scoring logic.
  • Accessibility & Deployment: Recognizing that schools and hackathon venues often face unreliable Wi-Fi, we engineered the game to run directly in any standard web browser with zero installation, alongside a standalone offline-capable build, and released it as free, open-source software for the broader community.
